extracted.intended_audience: seminarians, theology students, and Catholic theologians
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the formal effects and supernatural concomitants of sanctifying (habitual) grace in Catholic dogmatic theology, including scriptural, patristic, and scholastic arguments and points of controversy. The text treats sanctity, beauty, friendship with God, adoptive sonship, and four theses about infused virtues/gifts and the indwelling of the Holy Ghost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctity (formal effect of sanctifying grace)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first formal effect of sanctifying grace is sanctity: by the infusion of sanctifying grace sin is wiped out and sanctity is established in its place; justification involves both remission of sin and sanctification, and these are constitutive elements of habitual/sanctifying grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by Scripture (Eph. iv.24) and the Council of Trent’s definition of justification. The text explicates concrete manifestations: (a) the justified become living members of the mystical body of Christ (membrum vivum), (b) the faithful enjoy peace of heart and fortitude against flesh/world/devil, and (c) sanctifying grace entails a particular providence whereby God grants special assistance to preserve the state of grace (without violating free-will) and shields the just from bodily and spiritual danger (supported by Is. xlix.16, Rom. viii.28).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supernatural beauty of the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctifying grace beautifies the soul: the soul in the state of grace possesses a supernatural beauty that reflects the uncreated beauty of God and is likened by the Fathers to splendid painting, gold, a divine seal, and shining light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although modern aesthetics may ignore spiritual beauty, the Fathers and St. Thomas teach that grace 'beautifies like light' and that grace produces a new unity in the soul that manifests theological and moral virtues and the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost. The soul becomes, in a real sense, an image of the Trinity and a 'temple of the Holy Ghost,' participating in the Divine Nature and reflecting God's beauty; only God and the Elect fully perceive this, though pilgrims may sense it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship of God (established by sanctifying grace)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctifying grace transforms the relation between God and man from servitude/enmity to genuine supernatural friendship: man becomes a friend of God, enabled to reciprocate love by means of habitual grace and theological charity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounded in Scripture and Trent (e.g., John xv; Wisdom vii). The text adapts Aristotle’s conditions for friendship—(1) two distinct persons, (2) pure benevolent love (amor benevolentiae), (3) mutual consciousness of affection, and (4) equality of rank or a created form of equality—to show how friendship with God obtains: (1) God and the soul, (2) pure benevolence from God and habitual charity in the soul, (3) God’s knowledge and the soul’s probable knowledge suffice for mutuality, and (4) grace elevates the soul (amicitia excellentiae) enabling a true relation of friendship despite ontological inequality. The friendship is sometimes compared to mystic marriage and is accompanied by community of life and a sharing in God’s goods (operative charity toward neighbor as substitute).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoptive sonship (filiatio adoptiva) as a formal effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctifying grace culminates in the adoption of the justified as children of God—an adopted sonship with claim to the paternal inheritance (the beatific vision); this is taught by Scripture and defined by Trent as inseparable from justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural proofs include Rom. viii; 1 John iii; Gal. iv. St. Thomas’ elements of adoption (the adopted is a stranger to the adopter, has no legal claim, gives consent, and is received with parental love) are applied analogically: adoption is gratuitous, confers a spiritual inheritance, presupposes the consent of the adult soul, and elevates the creature to participation in the Divine Nature. The text also distinguishes between the natural Son (Christ) and adopted sons (creatures): Christ cannot be adopted; adopted sonship is analogical and accidental. Debated issues include whether Old Testament just were adopted sons (Trent rejects denial) and whether adoptive sonship requires the personal indwelling of the Holy Ghost (see controversy between Scheeben and Granderath; Scheeben: sanctifying grace alone suffices though the indwelling perfects it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis I: Infusion of the three theological virtues with sanctifying grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Faith, hope, and charity are infused into the soul together with sanctifying grace (a proposition regarded by some theologians as de fide or at least fidei proxima).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by Trent’s teaching that in justification 'faith, hope, and charity' are received together with remission of sins. Scriptural backing: Rom. v.5; 1 Cor. xiii.13. Scholastic debate concerns the timing of infusion: some (Suarez, Ripalda, De Lugo) maintain the three are infused in process leading up to justification; St. Thomas and St. Bonaventure hold they are infused at the moment of justification itself; the Tridentine Council favors infusion at justification. Mortal sin destroys sanctifying grace and the habit of charity; faith and hope may persist longer, but loss of faith entails loss of hope and charity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis II: Infusion of the supernatural moral (cardinal) virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: With sanctifying grace there are also infused moral virtues (prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance)—supernatural counterparts to acquired moral virtues—so that intellect and will are governed toward the supernatural end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterized as a common and probable theological opinion. Scriptural intimations include Wisdom viii.7 and Ezekiel xi.19 (giving a 'heart of flesh'). Some Fathers attribute cardinal virtues to divine infusion (Augustine, Gregory). St. Thomas’ analogical argument: just as natural virtues flow from natural principles, theological virtues require corresponding supernatural habits proportionate to them; hence the infusion of moral virtues is fitting and probable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis III: Infusion of the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost
rubrics_metrics.description: The seven gifts of the Holy Ghost (wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, godliness/piety, and fear of the Lord) are also infused with sanctifying grace (a probable proposition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on Isaiah xi.2 and ecclesial practice (prayer 'Veni Sancte Spiritus'). The text surveys controversies: whether the gifts are distinct from infused moral virtues, whether they are habits or transient inspirations. The prevailing opinion presented is that the gifts are real, habitual dispositions distinct from theological and moral virtues, conferring a supernatural capacity to receive inspirations of the Holy Ghost and a readiness to obey His impulses in matters of salvation. Argument from Christ as mystical head (who had the gifts) implies members receive them by infusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis IV: Personal indwelling of the Holy Ghost as consummation of justification
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of justification culminates in the personal (substantial) indwelling of the Holy Ghost in the soul of the just; the indwelling may be considered the climax and consummation of created sanctifying grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes 'inhabitatio per dona accidentalia' (indwelling by created gifts/energeia) from 'inhabitatio substantialis sive personalis' (indwelling by uncreated substance). Scriptural attestations (John xiv; Rom. v; 1 Cor. iii & vi) and patristic testimony (esp. Eastern Fathers) support the substantial indwelling. Theologians agree on personal indwelling but differ as to manner: majority view holds the indwelling is not by hypostatic union or the soul-as-body relation, but is an objective indwelling of the whole Trinity appropriated to the Third Person (Holy Ghost as hypostatic holiness/personal love), so that the state of grace bears a special relation to the Holy Ghost while expressing communion with the whole Trinity. Fathers (Athanasius, Basil, Cyril, Augustine) are cited in support.
